name: Mandatory liability insurance proposals
blurb: Regimes requiring minimum cover before a high risk system may be deployed.

points.desc: RAND directs its recommendations at state regulators and the NAIC and says further federal legislation is not warranted, citing the states' authority over insurance under the McCarran Ferguson Act. It notes that Executive Order 14365 of December 2025 seeks to constrain state AI laws, and that the NAIC responded by asking the administration to affirm state regulation of AI in insurance. The question was unresolved when the report was written.
points.name: RAND argues against a federal mandate for now

summary: Regimes requiring minimum cover before a high risk system may be deployed.

part_3_high_value_red_flags: Broad professional services exclusions that treat AI system design or deployment as a professional service and remove coverage.
Cyber exclusions that eliminate coverage for data breaches or security failures caused by the AI system.
Sublimits for technology errors and omissions that are far below the mandatory minimum limit.
Exclusions for bodily injury or property damage arising from autonomous vehicles or robotics if the AI system controls physical movement.
Punitive or exemplary damages exclusions that may conflict with mandatory regime requirements.
Prior acts exclusions that bar coverage for claims arising from AI system versions deployed before the policy inception.
Contractual liability exclusions that remove coverage for indemnities the insured has given to customers.
manuscript_wording_and_carve_backs: Delete or narrow the professional services exclusion to clarify that AI system deployment is not a professional service.
Add a specific endorsement covering algorithmic discrimination and bias claims within the bodily injury and property damage definition.
Remove any cyber exclusion that would bar coverage for data breaches caused by the AI system's failure.
Include a contractual liability endorsement to cover indemnities given to customers for AI system failures.
Add a prior acts endorsement to cover claims arising from AI system versions deployed before the policy inception.
Negotiate a punitive damages carve back where insurable by law, to meet mandatory regime requirements.
Add a defence costs in addition to limits of liability endorsement to preserve the full limit for damages.

part_4_program_structure_and_limits.bi_waiting_period: Business interruption waiting periods for third party claims are not standard in liability policies, but if the mandatory regime includes contingent business interruption, a waiting period of 24 to 72 hours is typical.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.business_interruption: Third party business interruption claims from AI system downtime are a growing exposure, and underwriters will want to see how the mandatory minimum limit addresses loss of use or loss of profits.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.property_eb_equipment: Equipment breakdown coverage for the AI system's own hardware is not part of the mandatory liability requirement but may be purchased separately to protect the insured's balance sheet from first party losses.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.per_occurrence_primary_excess_layered_pr: For third party property damage claims arising from the AI system, the primary layer usually carries a per occurrence limit of five to ten million dollars, with excess layers stacked above.

part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.cgl_primary: A commercial general liability policy may provide a base but will likely need manuscript endorsements to cover AI specific exposures, as standard CGL excludes professional services and often cyber.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.paper_basis: Claims made basis applies here because the mandatory liability insurance proposal for high risk AI systems typically requires coverage for claims first made during the policy period, reflecting the long tail nature of algorithmic failures.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.excess_umbrella_towers: Excess and umbrella towers above the mandatory minimum are usually structured in layers of five to ten million dollars each, with follow form wording to the primary AI liability policy.

part_1_core_third_party_liability_exposu: Bodily injury or property damage caused by autonomous decisions or physical actions of the AI system.
Discrimination or bias claims from individuals affected by automated decisions in credit, employment, or public services.
Privacy violations from improper data use or security breaches involving the AI system.
Failure to perform or software defect claims from customers relying on the AI system's outputs.
Intellectual property infringement by the AI system's training data or generated content.
Regulatory enforcement actions and associated defence costs.
Product liability if the AI system is embedded in a physical product.

underwriter_wants_to_know: Which jurisdiction's mandatory insurance regime applies and what minimum limit and scope of cover it prescribes.
The exact definition of high risk AI system under the applicable law and whether the insured's system meets that threshold.
The insured's risk management and testing protocols for the AI system before deployment.
Historical loss experience or claims data for similar AI systems in the same sector.
Whether the mandatory regime requires occurrence based or claims made coverage and any retroactive date requirements.
The insured's contractual indemnities and liability caps with customers and end users.
The potential for regulatory fines or penalties that may not be insurable under the mandatory minimum.
